title: Foot and ankle examination: suspected Achilles tendon rupture

guidelineVersions: MHRA Drug Safety Update on fluoroquinolones (January 2024)
Myhrvold et al., NEJM (2022); UKSTAR, Lancet (2020)

related.why: Neuropathy, ischaemia, infection and Charcot foot

brief.scenario: Mr Idris Belcourt, 41, an accountant, felt as if someone had kicked the back of his right heel while playing badminton five days ago. He is walking with a limp. His GP diagnosed an ankle sprain.
brief.task: Examine his feet and ankles. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to present your findings and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Walk and stand (heel raise), look and feel the tendon, then prone: resting angle and calf squeeze; then neurovascular.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Accepting active plantarflexion as proof the tendon is intact: the long toe flexors and tibialis posterior can still do it.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Could you take off both shoes and socks and walk for me?"

flow: Consent, expose both legs below the knee

grid.label: Preparation and exposure
grid.fail: Examines the right ankle only, with a sock on.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, gains consent, asks about pain, and exposes both legs below the knee, shoes and socks off.
grid.high: Explains he'll lie face down for part of it and compares with the left leg throughout.

grid.label: Gait and standing
grid.fail: Examines him only lying on the couch.
grid.pass: Watches his gait; inspects both legs from behind standing; asks for a single-leg heel raise on each side.
grid.high: Notes a flat-footed gait without push-off and inability to heel raise on the right.

grid.label: Look and feel
grid.fail: Doesn't palpate the tendon along its length.
grid.pass: Looks for swelling, bruising and a visible gap; palpates the tendon from calf to heel for a gap and tenderness.
grid.high: Also palpates the malleoli, navicular and base of the fifth metatarsal to screen for a fracture.

grid.label: Calf squeeze and resting angle (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Accepts active plantarflexion as proof the tendon is intact.
grid.pass: Prone, feet over the couch edge: resting angle (Matles) and calf squeeze (Simmonds), comparing sides.
grid.high: Knows the calf squeeze is sensitive (0.96) and that at least two tests were positive in every rupture in the key series.

grid.label: Neurovascular and ankle range
grid.pass: Checks dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, capillary refill, sensation including the sural nerve, and ankle and subtalar movement.
grid.high: Records sural nerve sensation before any surgery, because the nerve lies close to the tendon.

grid.label: Presentation at the signal
grid.pass: Presents an acute complete right Achilles tendon rupture: palpable gap, positive calf squeeze, no heel raise, neurovascularly intact.
grid.high: Adds that the rupture was missed, and asks about fluoroquinolone antibiotics and steroid injections.

grid.label: Immediate management (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Sends him home in a trainer with physiotherapy advice.
grid.pass: Same day: immobilise in equinus in a boot or cast, crutches, analgesia, VTE risk assessment, and specialist foot and ankle review.
grid.high: Considers LMWH for lower limb immobilisation when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, as NICE NG89 advises.

grid.label: Treatment options
grid.fail: Tells him surgery is the only way to walk normally again.
grid.pass: Non-operative functional treatment and surgery give similar function; surgery lowers re-rupture risk but adds wound and nerve complications.
grid.high: Re-rupture about 6% non-operative versus under 1% with surgery; a functional brace is as good as a cast.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Could you pop your right foot up on the couch? [Sock left on; examines lying only.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Squeezes the ankle.] A bit swollen. [Doesn't feel along the tendon.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Point your foot down. [He can.] So the Achilles is fine.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Home in his trainers with physiotherapy. If it's still bad, an operation is the only fix.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? I'd like to examine both feet and ankles. Is it sore now? Could you take off both shoes and socks and roll up your trousers? [Cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Could you walk for me? [Watches.] Now stand, and rise up on your left toes, then your right. [Can't on the right.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Looks from behind: swelling, bruising.] [Feels the tendon from calf to heel.] There's a tender gap above the heel.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Could you lie face down with your feet over the edge? [Right foot hangs more dorsiflexed.] [Squeezes each calf.] No plantarflexion on the right.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulses, capillary refill, sensation including the lateral foot, ankle and subtalar movement.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Belcourt has an acute complete right Achilles tendon rupture: a palpable gap, positive calf squeeze, abnormal resting angle and no single heel raise. He is neurovascularly intact.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Today I'd put him in a boot or cast in equinus, with crutches and analgesia, assess his VTE risk, and arrange foot and ankle review.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not necessarily. Function is similar either way; surgery lowers the re-rupture risk but has wound and nerve risks. We'd decide together.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. Can I check your name and date of birth? I'll look while you walk and stand, then ask you to lie face down, comparing both legs.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Gait.] He walks flat-footed with no push-off on the right, and can't do a single heel raise on that side.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Palpable gap above the heel.] I'll also press the malleoli, navicular and fifth metatarsal base. [Not tender.] No fracture signs.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Resting angle and calf squeeze positive.] He can still point his foot using the long toe flexors, which is why it's missed. The calf squeeze is highly sensitive, and here two tests are positive.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Pulses, capillary refill normal.] Sural nerve sensation normal: I record that before any surgery.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An acute complete right Achilles rupture, missed as a sprain. Have you taken antibiotics like ciprofloxacin recently, or had steroid injections?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Equinus boot or cast today, crutches, analgesia and a VTE assessment: NICE NG89 says consider LMWH for lower limb immobilisation if his VTE risk outweighs his bleeding risk.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A Norwegian trial found similar function at a year; re-rupture was about 6% without surgery and under 1% with it, but nerve injuries were commoner after surgery. UKSTAR showed a functional brace is as good as a cast. I'd share that and let him choose.

failures.consequence: Safety-critical: the rupture is missed, the ends drift apart and later reconstruction may be needed.
Misses the loss of heel raise and push-off.

failures.move: Discharging without equinus immobilisation or VTE assessment.
failures.consequence: The tendon heals long, and a preventable VTE risk goes unassessed.

failures.move: Presenting surgery as the only option.
failures.consequence: Denies shared decision-making when outcomes are similar.

recovery.line: Could you stand and try to rise up on your toes, one foot at a time?
If I'm unsure, I'd treat it as a rupture in equinus and arrange ultrasound.

knowledge.fact: Calf squeeze: sensitivity 0.96, specificity 0.93. Matles: 0.88 and 0.85. Palpable gap: 0.73 and 0.89.
Non-operative versus surgery: similar function at 12 months; re-rupture 6.2% versus 0.6%; more nerve injuries after surgery.
Non-operative: functional brace with early weight-bearing is as good as a plaster cast.
Lower limb immobilisation: consider LMWH if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk.
Fluoroquinolones cause tendinitis and rupture; avoid with corticosteroids; caution over 60.
Suspected acute Charcot foot: non-weight-bearing and urgent multidisciplinary foot service referral.

recall.think: Is the tendon ruptured, even though he can point his foot?
do: Feel for a gap; prone resting angle

numbers.meaning: sensitivity of the calf squeeze test

recall.trap: Active plantarflexion doesn't exclude a rupture.
recall.finish: Equinus boot or cast, VTE assessment; shared decision on non-operative or surgical treatment.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, obtain consent and clean hands at every station; 6-minute signal in examination stations

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Foot and ankle examination (gait, heel raise, palpation, movements); Achilles tendon rupture: clinical features, immobilisation in equinus, sural nerve relation to the tendon; bony landmarks for ankle and midfoot fracture

sources.name: Maffulli N. The clinical diagnosis of subcutaneous tear of the Achilles tendon. A prospective study in 174 patients. Am J Sports Med 1998;26(2):266–70
sources.supports: Sensitivity: calf squeeze 0.96, Matles 0.88, palpable gap 0.73; specificity: calf squeeze 0.93, Matles 0.85, gap 0.89; at least two tests positive in all patients with a rupture

sources.name: Myhrvold SB, et al. Nonoperative or surgical treatment of acute Achilles' tendon rupture. N Engl J Med 2022;386(15):1409–20
sources.supports: No difference in Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score at 12 months between nonoperative treatment, open repair and minimally invasive surgery; re-rupture 6.2% nonoperative vs 0.6% in each surgical group; nerve injury 5.2% minimally invasive, 2.8% open, 0.6% nonoperative

sources.name: Costa ML, et al. Plaster cast versus functional brace for non-surgical treatment of Achilles tendon rupture (UKSTAR): a multicentre randomised controlled trial and economic evaluation. Lancet 2020;395(10222):441–8
sources.supports: No difference in function at 9 months or re-rupture between plaster cast and functional brace with early weight-bearing

sources.name: NICE NG89: Venous thromboembolism in over 16s: reducing the risk of hospital-acquired deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
sources.supports: Consider pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH or fondaparinux for people with lower limb immobilisation whose risk of VTE outweighs their risk of bleeding (1.11.1)

sources.name: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics: must now only be prescribed when other commonly recommended antibiotics are inappropriate (22 January 2024)
sources.supports: Tendinitis and tendon rupture with fluoroquinolones; special caution over 60 years, renal impairment or solid-organ transplant; avoid use with corticosteroids; report suspected adverse reactions via the Yellow Card scheme

sources.name: NICE NG19: Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management
sources.version: Published 26 August 2015; last updated 11 October 2019 (minor changes September 2024)
sources.supports: Suspected acute Charcot arthropathy: refer to the multidisciplinary foot care service and keep non-weight-bearing meanwhile (1.7.3)

partner.opening: Please examine this gentleman's feet and ankles. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mr Idris Belcourt, 41, an accountant. Five days ago at badminton you felt a kick to the back of your right heel and heard a snap. You can walk but limp. Your GP said it was a sprain. No regular medicines; you took ciprofloxacin for a urine infection last month. Point your foot down if asked. Don't rise onto your right toes when asked to heel raise.

reveals.trigger: Watches him walk and stand; asks for heel raises
reveals.finding: Flat-footed gait with no push-off on the right. Can't do a single heel raise on the right; left normal.

reveals.trigger: Looks and palpates the tendon and bony landmarks
reveals.finding: Swelling and bruising around the right heel. Tender, palpable gap in the tendon a few centimetres above the heel. Malleoli, navicular and fifth metatarsal base not tender.

reveals.trigger: Prone: resting angle and calf squeeze
reveals.finding: Right foot hangs in more dorsiflexion than the left. Calf squeeze: no plantarflexion on the right; normal on the left. Active plantarflexion present but weak.

reveals.trigger: Checks pulses, sensation and ankle movement
reveals.finding: Pulses and capillary refill normal. Sensation normal, including the lateral foot. Ankle and subtalar movement full, apart from painful plantarflexion.
Say: "Please stop there and present your findings."

push.question: He can point his foot down. How can the tendon be ruptured?
push.expect: Long toe flexors, tibialis posterior and peronei can still plantarflex; calf squeeze and resting angle test the tendon.

push.question: What do you do today?
push.expect: Equinus boot or cast, crutches, analgesia, VTE risk assessment, foot and ankle review.

push.question: Should he have surgery?
push.expect: Shared decision: similar function; surgery lowers re-rupture but adds wound and nerve risk.

curveballs.prompt: He mentions he took ciprofloxacin last month.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Fluoroquinolones cause tendon rupture: record it as a likely contributor and report on a Yellow Card.

curveballs.prompt: The examination is equivocal and he has marked swelling.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treat as a rupture in equinus and arrange ultrasound.

curveballs.prompt: He presents six weeks after the injury instead.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Delayed rupture: specialist foot and ankle opinion, as reconstruction may be needed.

curveballs.prompt: A patient with diabetes has a hot, swollen foot with intact skin and no clear injury.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspect acute Charcot foot: keep non-weight-bearing and refer to the multidisciplinary foot service (see MB-214).
